job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in structural engineering, so mornings are lectures and afternoons are the library, working through a design for a footbridge. I live with my mum in a flat in Hartley. She drives the number 14 bus, and my sister Rosa is sixteen, so I'm usually the one making dinner. Saturdays I tutor maths for pocket money, because there's no spare cash and no one to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds about right, because the hype always outruns the real thing. I'd tell my course mates not to panic but also not to relax, because plateau doesn't mean a job is waiting for us. At the end of the day it's still who the firms decide to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a safer world for me than the others, but it's no cure for money. I have a heavy loan and about three weeks of living costs saved, and my mum can't help. The bridge and road firms around Hartley might hire two or three juniors this year, and there are a few hundred of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the Saturday tutoring and apply to about forty firms, including the inspection company where I interned, Calder & Wynn. I'd ask the manager there, Mrs Adeyemi, for a reference and a coffee. I'd also keep paying a small part of the loan even while studying, so it doesn't balloon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty tense. I'm not scared of the world, I'm scared of the arithmetic. I look at my phone's banking app more than I'd like to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no spare cash at home. Which bill would worry you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent at home is covered, so the first thing to give would be Rosa's school trip money, which I help with. Then my own lunches. I'd be ashamed telling her, so I'd probably just say there's no space in the budget this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What do you actually use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for checking spreadsheets and formulas, and to summarise long design codes. I don't trust it for a final answer. In structural work if something's wrong a bridge cracks, so I check each number twice, whatever the tool says.

say: I'd tell course mates plateau is **no cure** for money, because it still comes down to who firms hire.
I'd say good infrastructure jobs need **public investment**, not hype.
think: A plateau is safer for me, but my loan and **three weeks of savings** are the real pressure.
Only two or three local firms hire juniors, and there are a **few hundred** of us.
do: Apply to about **40 firms**, starting with Calder & Wynn where I interned.
Keep the Saturday **maths tutoring** while I study.
Ask Mrs Adeyemi (my old internship manager) for a **reference**.
feel: **Tense** about money, not scared of the world.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of the world, I'm scared of the arithmetic.
fieldNote: Money, not technology, is his main worry; he's the quiet family fixer.
Cautious and **evidence-led** with AI: uses it, but checks every number twice.
Helps his sister Rosa with school costs, so any shortfall touches her.

steps.text: Apply to 40 structural and highway firms by spring
Keep the Saturday maths tutoring job
Pay a small part of the loan each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the government has to step in. Companies will use it to hire fewer juniors and call it progress, and shareholders will cheer. I'd back a public works programme because bridges, rail and flood defences need building, and they're the kind of jobs that get people into work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the first rung of the ladder is the first thing that goes. The routine checking, load calculations and drawing updates I did on my internship are what software does well now. I'd guess firms hire two juniors where they'd hire five, and I need to be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools more on purpose. Learn to run its calculations and then check them by hand, so I'm the person who can say when it's wrong. I'd also ask Calder & Wynn about site inspection work, because they need people at the bridge itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit frustrated at who gets rewarded, and a bit interested in the new tools. I'd sleep okay if I had a job lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a junior structural engineer's job do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calculation checks and drawing updates. Things like checking a beam against a code takes me an afternoon, and a tool does it in minutes. What stays is judgement: walking a site, seeing a crack and deciding whether it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa if she asked whether to study engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her yes, but pair it with a trade skill, like site experience or surveying, and keep her loan small. And I'd tell her to join a union early. I'd want her to have more cover than I do.

say: I'd call for **public works** like bridges, rail and flood defences to give graduates real jobs.
I'd say companies and **shareholders** will profit while juniors lose their first rung.
think: Firms might hire **two juniors** where they once hired five, and I must be one of them.
Calculation checks are what tools do well; **site judgement** stays human.
do: Learn to run **AI calculations** and then check them by hand.
Ask Calder & Wynn about **site inspection** work at bridges.
Join the **union** for engineers as a student member.
feel: **Frustrated** about who gets rewarded, but curious about the new tools.
S1.quote: What stays is judgement: walking a site, seeing a crack and deciding whether it matters.
fieldNote: Looks for the human part of the job: **judgement** on site.
Blames shareholders and wants public works, in line with his progressive politics.
Steady learner: will adopt tools once they've proven themselves.

steps.text: Practise AI calculation tools and then check results by hand
Ask Calder & Wynn for site inspection work on bridges
Join the engineers' union as a student member

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to act at once, with a basic income and a pause on mass layoffs while we work this out. I'd join the demonstrations, and I'd tell people to get their families to talk about money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've picked the worst possible year to graduate. The calculations and design are thinking work, and they'd be gone by 2028, and I'm still paying off a loan. The only gap is inspection and site work, which might last till about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's thesis where it is and chase any paid site job I can find, even a trainee surveyor. I'd cut costs to the bone and move the loan to the lowest payments possible. And I'd tell my mum and Rosa the truth, rather than hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a heavy chest. I'd feel responsible for Rosa and for my mum, who's already tired. I think I'd sleep four hours a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves you finishing the master's right as it lands. What would you do that year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about moving out to where infrastructure repair is going on, even for short contracts. The council in Hartley has a bridge programme, so I'd go to every meeting. And I'd talk to my tutoring clients about taking more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots take the hands-on side three years later, does inspection work still protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes, but three years isn't a career. Inspecting bridges is what I'd do until about 2031, and then robots do the climbing. I'd use those years to stack up savings and think about a trade that stays human, maybe supervising or teaching.

say: I'd demand a **basic income** and a pause on mass layoffs until we work things out.
I'd join **demonstrations** and tell people to talk to their families about money now.
think: Design and calculation work could be **gone by 2028** while my loan remains.
Site inspection might **last until 2031**, but three years isn't a career.
do: Chase **any paid site job**, even trainee surveyor, rather than finish the thesis early.
Cut costs and move the loan to the **lowest payments**.
Tell my mum and Rosa **the truth** about money.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a heavy chest and short nights.
S2.quote: I'd feel responsible for Rosa and for my mum, who's already tired. I think I'd sleep four hours a night.
fieldNote: Family worry (his sister and mother) lifts his mood to **alarmed**.
Tries to use the three-year robot gap as a window to build savings.
Politics and practical steps run side by side.

steps.text: Take any paid trainee site or surveying job going
Cut costs and switch the loan to the lowest payments
Go to demonstrations and council meetings about the bridge programme
Tell my mum and Rosa the plan and ask for patience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build real protections, like retraining funds and a public jobs programme. I'd write to my MP and push my union to make a graduate guarantee. It's a fight, but it can be won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still anxious, but I feel I can act. By 2031 I might have three years of work on a bridge or road job and some loan paid down. If I'm good with the tools, I'd be one of the people who checks what the machines produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent graduate job, probably in inspection, put a third of every pay cheque on the loan and then keep using AI tools to speed up the dull bits. I'd also start learning a hands-on skill like surveying that stays useful after 2034. And I'd save for Rosa's first year at university, if she wants to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled than the two-year one. There's a clock but it's one I can read. I'd still have mornings where I look at the loan balance and feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the five-year version change about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan is fixed, so it's about clearing it faster. If I'm working by 2027 and I put a third of my pay on the loan, I could cut it by half before 2031. That would let me choose my next move rather than being pushed into one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope your mum gets, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pension she can count on and a bus route that isn't automated away. She says the driving is the best bit of her day, and I'd hate to see that go. I'd be happy with a rule that people get help first, before profits.

say: I'd write to my MP and push for **retraining funds** and a graduate jobs guarantee.
I'd say five years is a **fight** that can be won.
think: By 2031 I could have **three working years** and a smaller loan.
I'd aim to be a person who **checks** what the machines produce.
do: Take the first decent **inspection job** and put a third of each cheque on the loan.
Learn **surveying**, a hands-on skill that outlasts 2034.
Save for **Rosa's first year** at university.
feel: **Settled but watchful**; there's a clock, but one he can read.
S3.quote: If I'm working by 2027 and I put a third of my pay on the loan, I could cut it by half before 2031.
fieldNote: Time converts his fear into a **financial plan** with real numbers.
Cares about his mother's bus-driving job, which could be automated.
Family-plans tag from helping his sister toward university.

steps.text: Take the first decent inspection job and put a third of pay on the loan
Learn surveying, a hands-on skill that outlasts 2034
Save for Rosa's first year at university
Write to my MP about a graduate jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the decade wisely: build the public jobs programme, train people, and make companies pay in. It's a long time, but long times get wasted if nobody pushes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm okay, to be honest. Ten years is a full career in which I'd pay the loan, save and perhaps own a flat. The thinking side will change, so I'd have to keep learning, but I'd be doing it from a stable job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, take a job at a firm like Calder & Wynn, clear the loan by thirty and use AI tools every week. I'd also pursue a chartered engineer qualification, which needs site experience and stays valuable. And I'd help Rosa through university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. I'd still worry about people with less, but personally I could breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What does your life look like if it goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chartered, a flat of my own, a couple of years of savings and Rosa finishing her degree. My mum could drop to part-time. I'd be the one who looks after the family, which I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world you'd still lose sleep over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who aren't in a position to retrain. My mum is fifty-five and she's not going to learn to code. I'd want something decent set aside for people like her. I'd vote for whoever promises it.

say: I'd say the **decade** must be used to build public jobs, training and company contributions.
I'd say **long times** get wasted if nobody pushes.
think: Ten years is a **full career**, with the loan cleared and maybe a flat.
I'd worry less for myself and more for people who **can't retrain**.
do: Take a firm job and clear the **loan by 30**.
Pursue the **chartered engineer** qualification that needs site experience.
feel: **Fairly good**, with some guilt for people with less.
S4.quote: My mum is fifty-five and she's not going to learn to code. I'd want something decent set aside for people like her.
fieldNote: Only here does he feel his own job is **safe enough**; mood falls to uneasy.
Concern shifts to his mother and others who can't retrain.
Plans around professional chartership as long-term armour.

steps.text: Join a firm like Calder & Wynn and clear the loan by 30
Work toward chartered engineer status with site experience

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It lands exactly when I finish and have a loan and no cushion. What would help most is a guaranteed graduate placement on public works, and loan payments that pause if you can't find work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell my mum. I'd tell my mum the truth, even if it hurts, because she's lied to herself for years about bills and it hasn't helped. I'd rather we all had the same plan.

headlineQuote: I'd tell my mum the truth, even if it hurts, because she's lied to herself for years about bills and it hasn't helped.
portrait: David is a **24-year-old** top civil graduate doing a master's in structural engineering, living with his mother and sister in Hartley.
He carries a **heavy loan** and no family help, so money worries drive him more than AI itself.
He's a steady learner who uses AI tools now and then and checks every number twice.
His mood ranges from **anxious** to alarmed, and eases only when ten years give him time.
He blames shareholders, backs public works and a union, and puts his mother and sister first.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it hits right as he finishes with a loan and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **public-works placement** for graduates and loan payments that pause when you can't find work.
